1:
All of them mark the turn from doctrine to practice, and Calvin makes it a claim about method. It is vain to form the life aright without first proving that the origin of all righteousness in men is in God and Christ. This, he says, is the main difference between the gospel and philosophy: the philosophers speak excellently about morals, but whatever shines in their precepts is a beautiful superstructure without a foundation, a mutilated doctrine like a body without a head — and the schoolmen of his own day come nearer the heathen philosophers than the apostles. Barnes draws a different consequence from the same therefore: none of the doctrines of the gospel are meant to be cold and barren speculations, and it is clear the apostle never supposed the doctrines of grace tended to licentiousness, though many have said that justification by faith, election and perseverance do. Ellicott, interested in the seam rather than the logic, imagines the apostle pausing in his dictation at the climax of the argument and not resuming until another sitting — the sequence being as much one of feeling as of reasoning. Clarke prefaces the chapter with a numbered recapitulation: that the believing Gentiles have a clear title to the covenant, that this right stands on the same footing as Abraham\'s, and that the grace given in Christ agrees with the deliverance from death bestowed on all mankind.

That Paul entreats where he might command is noticed by three schools. Chrysostom observes that so great a person does not decline beseeching, not for anything he was likely to gain himself but for what they would gain; the mercies of God themselves take the attitude of suppliants, as though a man wishing to move someone who had received great kindness were to bring the benefactor himself as a suppliant. Theodoret says the same: he lays down laws but sinks his authority and puts his instructions forward with entreaties. Henry adds the pastoral reason: though he might command, for love's sake he rather beseeches, and many are sooner wrought upon if accosted kindly, being more easily led than driven. Gill notes that brethren expresses the relation and the affection.

On the sacrifice they divide between grammar and image. Robertson identifies the verb as the technical term for offering a sacrifice, and glosses the last phrase as worship rendered by the reason or soul — with the aside that the same word elsewhere means not logical milk but the milk that nourishes the soul. Chrysostom explains why living had to be added at once: having said sacrifice, the apostle had to prevent anyone supposing he bade them kill themselves. Ellicott insists that your bodies is not a periphrasis for yourselves but means the body strictly, the part of a man most apt to be an occasion of falling — and quotes Chrysostom for how a body becomes a sacrifice: let the eye look on no evil thing, the tongue speak nothing filthy, the hand do no lawless deed. Henry takes the opposite view, that the whole self is meant, expressed so because under the law it was the bodies of beasts that were offered; and the offering was sacrificed by the priest but presented by the offerer.

Wesley alone reads the verse as a deliberate recapitulation, matching each phrase to something earlier. The mercies of God stands opposed to the wrath of God, your bodies to the vile abuse of their bodies, living to the life of the just by faith, holy to what the holy law requires, acceptable to the impossibility of pleasing God in the flesh. The last phrase he turns into a comparison: the worship of the heathen was utterly unreasonable and so was the glorying of the Jews, but a Christian acts in all things by the highest reason, inferring his duty from the mercy of God.
2:
The English pair conformed and transformed looks like a play on words, and Ellicott warns that it is not: the two Greek words are distinct, and the difference is between an outward conformity or disguise and a thorough inward assimilation. Robertson takes the first as a present imperative with a negative, meaning stop being fashioned, and puts it in a phrase of his own — do not take this age as your fashion plate. Clarke renders the second as metamorphosed or transfigured, a radical change both outward and inward, and supports it from a pagan quarter, quoting Seneca that he perceived himself not merely amended but transformed.

What this world covers is disputed, partly on lexical grounds. Barnes notes that the word here is not the one normally rendered world but one denoting an age or generation, so the precept may be aimed at one idolatrous age or extended to every age alike. Ellicott makes it the state of the world at the coming of Christ, over against the new Messianic reign. Clarke allows both the Jewish economy and the manners of the Gentiles, warning against reviving usages that Christ had abolished. Gill offers the same alternative and then does what none of the others do: he qualifies the prohibition, since it does not touch dress and civil usage provided pride and luxury are guarded against and the different stations in life attended to. Clarke has no such reservation, listing pride, luxury, vanity and riotous living as prevailing now exactly as then. Barnes is franker still about applying the rule: many think they are not conformed to the world while easily perceiving that their neighbour is, indulging in things others count worldly and opposing things others think innocent.

On the renewing of the mind Calvin is sharpest. The renovation required is not of the flesh only, nor of the inferior part of the soul as the schoolmen explain it, but of the mind — the greatest part of us, and the part to which the philosophers ascribe supremacy, calling it the leading power and imagining reason a most wise queen. But Paul, he says, pulls her from her throne and reduces her to nothing by teaching that we must be renewed in mind; for however we flatter ourselves, every man must be born again who would enter the kingdom of God, in mind and heart being altogether alienated from the righteousness of God. Ellicott approaches the same faculty analytically: the mind is neutral in itself, an instrument of evil when informed by an evil principle and of good when informed by the Spirit, performing the discrimination that supplies the data to conscience — so that it is not conscience but the rational part of it, to which the moral quality must still be added. Clarke draws the practical order: let the inward change produce the outward, for where the temper and disposition of the mind are not renewed, an outward change is of little worth and short standing.

Theodoret alone asks why fashion is the right word for what is renounced. Wealth and power and the other pomps are called fashions because only future things are substances, alone permanent — the fashion of this world passeth away. He proves it from reversals: many have fallen from abundance into the extremest poverty, others sprung from the lowest parents have been entrusted with the noblest offices, and some who raised a haughty brow and thought themselves superior to everybody were suddenly carried off and became ill-savoured dust. Wesley closes on the purpose clause, taking the proving to be knowledge by sure trial, easily done by one who has presented himself to God, and the will of God to mean the whole preceptive part of Christianity, so excellently good and so perfective of our natures — adding that the non-conformity required is neither in judgment, spirit, nor behaviour.
3:
The grace by which the apostle speaks is taken by all for his office, not for any inward gift. Calvin makes the most of it: before specifying his command he reminds them of the authority given him, so that they might attend to his voice as to God's own — I speak not of myself, but as God's ambassador I bring you the commands entrusted to me — and so laid the Romans under the necessity of obeying unless they were prepared to despise God in the person of his minister. Gill and Clarke restrict the word to the apostleship, and Barnes adds why the warning was needed at Rome: the habit of judging there was by rank, wealth or office, and the church was in danger of judging by the same standard.

What follows is a play on words none can carry into English. Ellicott renders it woodenly to show the shape — not to be high-minded beyond what he ought to be minded, but to be minded unto sober-mindedness. Clarke calls it a paronomasia and takes the second verb apart, sound joined to mind, so that it means to think discreetly and modestly. Robertson notes the double play and draws a conclusion the others do not: self-conceit is a species of insanity. Theodoret, from a different age and school, arrives at the same place — by sobriety the apostle designates the healthy state of the mind, to teach us that arrogance is the sickness of the intellect — adding that in this he imitates his Master, who blessed the poor in spirit first.

The measure of faith supplies the standard, and Ellicott makes it graduated: each should propose a standard in proportion to the faith God has given him, so that the strongest faith may assume the highest standard and offer itself for the highest offices, and so on down the scale — provided the estimate is single-minded and not biased by self-love. Clarke takes faith here for the Christian religion itself. Theodoret says the word means grace, since by faith grace comes; Wesley points back to the earlier chapters, where the faith treated of is that from which all other gifts flow. Henry turns it into a warning that cuts both ways. As we must not be proud of our talents, so we must take heed lest under a pretence of humility we grow slothful in laying out ourselves for others. We must not say, I am nothing, therefore I will sit still and do nothing, but, I am nothing in myself, and therefore I will lay out myself to the utmost in the strength of the grace of Christ.

On the body Chrysostom finds two levellings and then a third. We are members one of another — not the small of the great only, but the great of the small — and we are all one body; and beyond both, the gift was of grace, so thou didst not take it, nor find it either. He then presses the vocabulary: the apostle does not say that one received more and another less, but that the gifts differ. Calvin draws the moral of contentment, that each should keep to his own capacity and not thrust himself into what belongs to others, Christ himself being the bond of a union men could not have made.

What it is to be one body in Christ divides them. Ellicott makes Christ the unifying principle of the Church as the will is in a man. Gill marks the body off from any body politic, one in Christ and not in Caesar. Barnes de-mystifies it: no physical or literal union, no destruction of personal identity, nothing unintelligible, and the sacred writers never intended such expressions to be explained literally — the union is the most tender in this world but no more mysterious than that which binds friend to friend.
6:
The most consequential note in the span is Wesley's on prophesying according to the proportion of faith. He takes prophecy here not as the extraordinary gift of declaring mysteries but as the ordinary gift of expounding scripture, and makes the measure a rule of interpretation: as the oracles of God, according to their general tenor, according to that grand scheme of doctrine delivered in them touching original sin, justification by faith and present inward salvation. There is a wonderful analogy between all these, he says, so that every article about which any question arises should be determined by this rule, and every doubtful scripture interpreted according to the grand truths that run through the whole. Ellicott takes prophesying differently, as referring to the more recondite portions of the faith, and Theodoret differently again, as covering not only foreknowledge of the future but the understanding of hidden things.

Whether ministry means the diaconate is a straight disagreement. Ellicott calls the word the technical term for the office of deacon, instituted for the practical business as opposed to the spiritual ministrations of the church, and covering alms, the poor and widows; Clarke says the same in a line. Barnes reviews the whole usage — of all classes of ministers as servants of Christ, of the apostles\' own work, and in a few places of the deacons\' office — and comes down the other way: he is inclined to think the apostle meant not deacons properly so called but those engaged in the ministry of the word.

Robertson marks a grammatical shift the others pass over. At he that teacheth the construction changes from the accusative to the nominative articular participle, so a verb has to be supplied for each clause that follows. He glosses the ruler as the one standing in front, diligence as haste in the sense of earnestness, and cheerfulness as a late word found nowhere else in the New Testament.

What the ruler rules divides them four ways. Calvin takes the word for those committed with the government of the church, the elders who presided and exercised discipline, and extends it to all kinds of governors. Ellicott makes it anyone holding a position of prominence, Wesley one that has the care of a flock. Clarke goes elsewhere: since the verb also means to defend or patronise, he thinks it signifies receiving and providing for strangers, especially the persecuted who had left their homes destitute, and perhaps entertaining the apostolic teachers who travelled about — the same word being used of Phoebe as a succourer of many.

Whether the last clauses name offices or duties is the sharpest division. Calvin insists they are offices: the givers are the deacons who dispensed the public charities, not men giving of their own property, and those who show mercy are the widows and others appointed to care for the sick, there being two distinct offices, to provide necessaries for the poor and to attend to their condition. Ellicott holds the opposite, that at this point the apostle passes from the definite functions of the ministry to what was common to all members, so that giving is to be taken in a wide sense. On simplicity he adds that it means singleness of motive, since he who gives to be seen of men exhausts the merit of the act.

On cheerfulness Calvin and Ellicott arrive independently at the same practical observation. Calvin: as nothing gives more solace to the sick than to see men cheerful in assisting them, so to observe sadness in the helper makes them feel themselves despised. Ellicott: the kindness of charity is doubled when done in a cheerful way, and there is a class of religious minds especially apt to forget it. Gill closes the list of speakers with a distinction of temperaments — some are Boanergeses, sons of thunder, and others Barnabases, sons of consolation.
9:
Calvin says the strongest thing about love without dissimulation. It is hard to express how ingenious almost all men are at pretending a love they do not have, for they deceive not only others but themselves, persuading themselves that they do not love amiss those whom they neglect and really slight; so that anyone may be a witness to himself whether he has anything in his heart opposed to love. Barnes makes a distinction the others pass over — the love of this verse is benevolence toward all mankind, the next verse brotherly love — and insists that genuine benevolence is not what professes attachment but what is shown in acts of kindness. Ellicott links the clauses through the word for unfeigned: love is to arise from genuine emotion, the basis of the character being an intense hatred of evil and as strong an adhesion to good. He then admits what the apostle does not supply — how those in whom these emotions are naturally weak may strengthen them — and offers the shortest advice, to become Christians.

Clarke traces the verb for abhorring to the Styx, the feigned river of hell by which the gods swore, any god who falsified the oath losing nectar and ambrosia for a century, so that the river was reputed hateful and the verb came to mean as hateful as hell. Robertson notes what holds the passage together: these are participles doing the work of imperatives, an idiom running on through the following verses.

On the affection of verse 10 they agree. Barnes says the word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and denotes the tenderness between parents and children, a word made for the occasion; Calvin says it bids brotherly love have in it the affection of parents and children. On preferring one another Ellicott suggests anticipating is nearer: the Christian takes the initiative and shows honour without waiting to receive it. Wesley supplies the method — consider habitually what is good in others and evil in yourselves — and Theodoret calls yielding the first place a proof of perfect love.

Whether the diligence of verse 11 is spiritual or practical divides them. Ellicott corrects the English: the word means zeal, and refers to the spiritual life. Gill agrees, taking it of the affairs of piety rather than the callings of life. Barnes and Clarke make it industry. Barnes holds that religion promotes industry, and concludes that an idle man and a Christian are names which do not harmonize. Clarke is blunter: the God who forbade working on the seventh day enjoined it on the other six, so he who neglects to labour during the week is as culpable as he who works on the Sabbath.

Fervency draws a metaphor from each. Ellicott takes the word in its etymological sense of boiling, comparing the Christian temperament to water bubbling over a flame, and adds that in spirit means not the Holy Spirit but the part of a man which is spirit. Theodoret makes it the spiritual grace given, to which alacrity is brought as fuel to a fire, the Spirit being quenched in those unworthy of it. Calvin says our flesh, like the ass, is always torpid and needs goads, and only the fervency of the Spirit can correct our sloth — answering the objection that though this fervency is God's gift it remains our duty to cherish the flame kindled from heaven, since for the most part the Spirit is suppressed through our own fault. On the last clause Clarke reports a well-attested variant reading serving the time rather than the Lord, for which most critics contend; Ellicott records it and dismisses it as no doubt wrong. Henry adds that God is served not only by working for him but by sitting still when he calls us to suffer, patience for God's sake being true piety.
12:
Wesley sets out the plan first: the chapter has dealt hitherto with faith and love, takes up hope here, and afterwards turns to duties toward others — saints, persecutors, friends, strangers and enemies. Theodoret binds the three clauses to what precedes: the man who is fervent in spirit obeys his Master readily and waits for the blessings looked for, rising superior to the temptations that befall him, arming himself with steadfastness and continually calling the divine grace to his assistance — which is what continuing instant in prayer means.

The word rendered distributing starts an argument about property. Barnes says it means having things in common, and that one of the most striking effects of Christianity was to loosen men's grasp on what they owned — but he marks the limit at once: the direction does not mean they were literally to hold all things in common, which would be to go back to savage barbarity, only that they were to be liberal with the needy. Ellicott takes saints to mean simply Christians and refers the precept to the well-known poverty of the early communities. Gill widens the circle before narrowing it: all men in want are to be relieved, even enemies, but especially they that are of the household of faith. Calvin puts the principle behind it most sharply. The chief duty of love is to do good to those from whom we expect the least recompense; and since those most pressed down with want are commonly the most despised, the benefits conferred on them being reckoned lost, God commends them to us particularly — for we prove our love genuine only when we relieve needy brethren for no other reason than to exercise our benevolence.

A textual variant here draws four voices and they converge remarkably. Some manuscripts and fathers read not necessities but memorials, so that the sense becomes taking part in the commemorations of the saints. Clarke reports the reading and dismisses it flatly: he cannot see any good sense it can make in the text, and keeps the common reading. Calvin's text calls it a depravation introduced by certain of the fathers to countenance the veneration of the monuments and sepulchres of martyrs, objecting that there were then no monuments of martyrs at Rome at all. Ellicott reaches the same diagnosis, that the allusion is to the later usage of holding festivals in honour of martyrs, and turns the case into a general argument: the best manuscripts are wonderfully free from corruptions of this kind, and even inferior ones admit them far less than might have been expected — the addition of and fasting in one gospel and of the doxology to the Lord's prayer being his other examples. Wesley arrives at the same controversy from the other direction, without any appeal to manuscripts, remarking that it is notable how the apostle, treating expressly of the duties that flow from the communion of saints, never says one word about the dead.

On hospitality the note that everyone takes is the force of the verb. Robertson glosses it as pursuing, as in a chase or hunt, and adds the play the Greek allows — they were to pursue hospitality as their enemies pursued them. Wesley says it means not only embracing the opportunities that offer but seeking them. Clarke supplies the circumstances that made the duty urgent: houses of public accommodation were scarce, the apostles were itinerants, and Christians were often flying before persecution — so that providing for strangers in distress is the proper meaning of the word. Theodoret widens it past the brethren, since the guests meant are not the saints only but such as have come from any quarter whatever and need entertainment.
14:
Chrysostom reads the order of the chapter as a campaign. Having joined the members closely into one, the apostle leads them out to the battle without, which is easier from this point — for he who has not managed matters well with his own side will find more difficulty with strangers. And he marks how far the command goes beyond the obvious: the apostle did not say, be not spiteful or revengeful, but required something far better, for that a wise man might do, whereas this is quite an angel's part. Calvin cautions that the reader is not to look for a precise order in these precepts, but must be content with short unconnected sayings deduced from the principle laid down at the chapter's opening.

Two notice that the command sounds like the Sermon on the Mount, and both stop short of calling it a quotation. Ellicott dates the coincidence: it was about the time this epistle was written that the compositions which became our gospels began, so the apostle need not have seen one — the Lord's teaching was at first circulated orally, and in that form he knew the precept to bless them that persecute you. Robertson arrives independently at the same verdict: like that passage in spirit, not a quotation but a reminiscence. Theodoret, writing long before either, had no such hesitation — this was a law of our Lord\'s, he says, for the Lord enjoined it upon the holy apostles. Barnes explains that cursing means properly to devote to destruction, and calls this one of the most difficult duties of the Christian religion, which nothing but religion will enable men to perform.

On weeping and rejoicing Calvin defines the failure at both ends: such is true love that a man would rather weep with his brother than look on his grief at a distance and live at ease, so that not to regard a brother's happiness with joy is envy, and not to grieve at his misfortunes is inhumanity. Ellicott makes an observation none of the older writers could have made: sympathy is more under the control of the will than might be supposed, becoming so by a conscious direction given to the whole life — and this injunction has been more fully carried out in modern times than most, having entered the social code and belonging as much to the gentleman as to the Christian, so that the danger now is that its expression should be unreal. Wesley notes that the direct opposite of weeping is laughter, but that this does not so well suit a Christian.

What being of the same mind requires is disputed, and Barnes gives his own rendering: seek for your brethren what you seek for yourself, and do not seek honours or offices for yourself that you do not seek for them. Gill guards the phrase from a misreading: it is not sameness of judgment or agreement in forms of discipline that is meant, but having the same love and thinking as well of others as of oneself. Theodoret glosses the next clause similarly: be not satisfied with your own judgments, but take the counsels of others also.

The last clause divides them. Ellicott thinks the common rendering right — let yourselves be carried along in the stream with those beneath you in rank, mixing freely and lending a hand, without letting social assumptions keep you at a distance — while noting the alternative, condescend to lowly things, which would commend the trivial round and the common task. Clarke delivers a verdict on the vice instead: attachment to high things and high men is the vice of little, shallow minds, such persons being conscious of no consequence in themselves and seeking credit by associating with rank. Let the poor, godly man be your chief companion, he says, and pass through life with as little noise as possible.
17:
Henry begins further back than the verse, with the reason retaliation comes so naturally: since men became enemies to God they have been very ready to be enemies one to another, and those who embrace religion must expect to meet enemies in a world whose smiles seldom agree with Christ's. His verdict on repaying evil is severe — that is a brutish recompence, befitting only animals, which are conscious of no being above them nor of any existence hereafter. Theodoret weighs the same command from the other end, as an achievement rather than a prohibition: to render no man evil for evil is an excellence belonging to virtue in its highest state of perfection, and approaching near to a total emancipation from the passions.

On providing things honest in the sight of all men the notes are practical. Wesley glosses the verb as thinking beforehand — contrive to give as little offence as may be to any. Theodoret sets beside it the apostle's own rule elsewhere, to give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God. Henry adds that we are not only to do but to study and take care to do what is amiable and creditable, so as to recommend religion to all with whom we converse.

The qualifications attached to living peaceably are what the commentators fasten on, and they read them as an admission. Barnes says the words imply that it cannot always be done, and draws out two duties from the second clause: we are to do our utmost to preserve peace and appease the anger of others, and we are never to begin or originate a quarrel — for their assaults we are not answerable, but we are answerable for our conduct towards them, and on no occasion are we to commence a warfare. Robertson renders the phrase literally as the part that proceeds from you, and quotes the summary that all our part is to be peace. Ellicott produces the decisive counter-example from the writer's own life, which was one of almost constant conflict, and concludes that peace plainly would not always be possible; the Christian can only be responsible for himself.

Clarke argues the duty from self-interest as much as from charity. To live at peace with neighbours, friends and even family is often very difficult, but the man who loves God must labour after it for his own sake, since no one can have broils and misunderstandings without having his own peace materially disturbed — he must, to be happy, be at peace with all men, whether they will be at peace with him or not. And the apostle knew the difficulty, which is why the double qualification stands in the text: though it be but barely possible, labour after it. Gill puts it in three verbs: peace is to be sought, pursued and cultivated.

Calvin alone treats peaceableness as a thing that can fail in two opposite directions, and states both cautions. Such a life, ordered so as to render us beloved by all, is no common gift, and to attain it a man needs not only perfect uprightness but courteous and kind manners, which may conciliate the just and good and make a favourable impression even on the hearts of the ungodly. But first, we are not to seek such esteem as would make us refuse to undergo anyone's hatred for Christ when that becomes necessary — and he observes that some who render themselves amicable to all by sweetness of manner are nevertheless hated by their nearest connections on account of the gospel. And second, courteousness must not degenerate into compliance, so as to lead us to flatter the vices of men for the sake of preserving peace. It is because peace with all men cannot always be had that the two exceptions are annexed to the command.
19:
Calvin turns the prohibition positive before the text does. We fulfil the precepts of not revenging only when we go beyond abstaining from injury to doing good, for it is a kind of indirect retaliation to turn our kindness aside from those who have wronged us. He also defines the term: the enemy meant is not one whom we regard with hatred but one who entertains enmity towards us — and if such are to be helped according to the flesh, much less is their salvation to be opposed by imprecating vengeance on them.

The coals of fire are read three ways and none of them comfortably. Ellicott notes that the same phrase elsewhere describes the divine vengeance, and takes it here metaphorically — thou shalt take the best and most summary vengeance upon him — while allowing an underlying idea of awakening shame and remorse. Robertson identifies the word behind anthracite and calls it a metaphor for keen anguish, comparing the Arab proverbs about coals in the heart and fire in the liver, adding that such kindness may lead to repentance. Calvin reports the same division, some understanding the destruction that returns on the enemy's head when he is treated better than he deserves and his guilt is doubled. Wesley cuts through with a quatrain about smelting: so artists melt the sullen ore of lead by heaping coals of fire upon its head, and in the kind warmth the metal learns to glow, and pure from dross the silver runs below. Theodoret alone names the danger in the harsher reading and refuses it: we are not to minister to our enemies in order that they may suffer the heavier retribution hereafter.

On the closing verse Barnes makes the largest claim in the chapter. To be overcome of evil is to let the temper be excited and Christian principle abandoned; to overcome evil with good is to subdue it by kindness and disarm the adversary of his rage. This, he says, is the noble and grand sentiment of the Christian religion — nothing like it is found in the heathen classics, and nothing like it ever existed among pagan nations. Robertson, glossing the same verse, quietly cites Seneca for it.

Clarke supplies the mechanism, and it is the most detailed thing here. A moral enemy is more easily overcome by kindness than by hostility, for against hostility he arms himself and all the evil passions of his heart concentrate against the man trying to retaliate; but where the injured man labours to do him good for his evil, his passions have no longer any motive, his mind relaxes, the turbulence is calmed, reason and conscience are permitted to speak, and he is disarmed — or rather finds he has no use for his weapons. He cites too the scholastic maxim that he is overcome of evil who sins against another because that other sinned against him.

The others state the principle as a paradox about victory. Ellicott: the infliction of vengeance is a sign not of strength but of weakness, and to repress the desire for revenge is a victory over self, nobler and also more effectual, since it disarms the enemy and turns him into a friend. Calvin: if we retaliate perverseness we confess ourselves overcome by it, whereas returning good for evil shows the invincible firmness of the mind — and he who tries to overcome evil with evil may surpass his enemy in doing injury, but to his own ruin, for by acting so he carries on war for the devil. Gill distinguishes three evils not to be overcome by — the evil one, indwelling sin, and the man who did the injury — warning that if we return evil for evil, not we but the wrongdoer is the conqueror. Wesley adds what the others leave out: if you see no present fruit, yet persevere.
